en: The Tiantai Diagram of Classifications divides this [subject] into two general sections;
first, the explanation of... [text missing].

Regarding the subsequent [section], the initial exposition on the arising of the teaching can be divided into two parts. First, a general clarification of all the sūtras, which is further divided into three: (1) because it fulfills their original vows; (2) because it responds to the arrival of requests;

and (3) because it accords with the fundamental capacities of sentient beings. This section is further divided into three: first, the explanation of the translated title; second, the discernment of its essence and characteristics, which is divided into four: (1) the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint); (2) the *pratyātma-pudgala-siddhānta* (standpoint for each individual);

(3) the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (standpoint of remedial treatment); and (4) the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (standpoint of ultimate truth). This [fourth] is further divided into two: (1) regarding that which is inexpressible; and (2) regarding that which is expressible. Third, the clarification of the motivation (*nidāna*).

Regarding the subsequent detailed explanation of this sutra among all teachings and practices, it is divided into four parts: first, explaining the two kinds of liberation; second, establishing the principle of the Pure Land;

third, manifesting the merit of those who hear the *Vimalakīrti*; and fourth, accomplishing the supreme offering. In explaining the two kinds of liberation, there are three sections: first, the pillar of liberation through true nature (*dharmatā*); second, the pillar of liberation through actual wisdom (*prajñā*); and third, the pillar of liberation through skillful means (*upāya*). Second, regarding the translation: it is said that during the reigns of nine successive dynasties, this work was translated six times;

this present version is the fifth translation. As for the "nine dynasties," they refer to the period following the Later Han: first, the Han; second, [the Wei]; third, [the Jin]; fourth, [the Liu Song]; fifth, [the Qi]; sixth, [the Liang]; seventh, [the Northern Zhou]; eighth, [the Sui]; and ninth, [the Tang]. (The text continues with the specific details of the translations.)

The Wei dynasty was the third; the Three Jin dynasties, the fourth; Song, the fifth; Qi, the sixth; Liang, the seventh; Zhou, the eighth; Sui, the ninth; and Tang, the tenth. When Cao [Yuan] spoke of "the shifting of times over a thousand years," he meant that customs undergo a single transformation.

When he spoke of "six translations," although the texts may lack a systematic classification, I fear that those newly entering the study will find it difficult to comprehend; thus, I shall briefly provide an exposition to clarify their divisions into six periods: first, the translations by the Liu family; second, the translations by the Sun family of the Wu court;

third, the translations by the Western Sima family and others; fourth, the translations by the Wang family of Eastern Jin and others; fifth, the translations by Yao Xing and Kumārajīva of Later Qin; and sixth, the translations by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty. These three are the orthodox.
The Explanation of the Sūtra’s Revealing Sections is divided into two parts.
First, the individual [commentaries], namely: (1) the section on Vimalakīrti and the section on the Inconceivable Dharma; (2) the nine sections by Master Sengzhao:

(a) the principle of emptiness, (b) the marvelous and divine, (c) the commentary by Master Sengzhao, (d) the commentary by Master Sengrui, (e) the ancient commentaries from within the Passes, (f) the commentary by Master Fotudeng, (g) the commentary by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, which is divided into two: (i) non-separation and (ii) separation; (h) the Three Treatises.

The Master’s *Commentary on the Ninefold Tiantai Exegesis* is divided into three parts: I. Distinguishing the Conceivable from the Inconceivable (7 sections): 1. Regarding Principle; 2. Regarding Wisdom; 3. Regarding Cessation; 4. Regarding the Realms; 5. Regarding Having Substance and Lacking Substance;
6. Regarding Having Function and Lacking Function; 7. Regarding the Common and the Uncommon. II. Specifically Judging and Explaining Inconceivable Liberation (3 sections):

1. Direct Nature Liberation; 2. Actual Wisdom Liberation; 3. Expedient Means Liberation. III. Categorizing and Generalizing Across All Dharmas (Briefly divided into 11 sections): 1. The Three Paths; 2. The Two Consciousnesses; 3. ... [and so forth].

Three Natures; Four [Truths]; Three Kinds of Prajñā; Five Kinds of Bodhi; Three Kinds of Mahāyāna; Three Kinds of Dharmakāya; Three Kinds of Nirvāṇa; Nine [Topics]; One Essence and Three Jewels; Thirteen Virtues.
Following this, the general introduction to the present preface is presented.
Within this, there are two parts. First, the sequence of the arising of the teaching, which is further divided into three sections.
The first four lines concern the origin of the teaching’s emergence; the second concerns how previous translations were not fully harmonized.

Third, this present work clarifies the principles through its thoroughness. Second, explaining the reasons for providing this commentary is divided into two parts: first, explaining the reasons for the commentary, which has two sub-sections. First, expressing regret that the present age has lost the original intent serves as the remote cause;

second, praising the ancients for their attainment of the truth serves as the proximate cause. Following these, the main explanation of the commentary is divided into three parts. First, stating words of humility.

The passage beginning with "I, Dao-li, not presuming upon my own meager abilities," etc., records the date; the passage beginning with "the first year of Shangyuan," etc., constitutes the subsequent chapter on the benefits of the Dharma;
and the passage beginning with "may the Dharma further become clear," etc., is the ancient preface.

Within this, there are four sections. First, the general clarification of the *hon* (original) and *soku* (traces). This section penetrates all sutras and is divided into two parts. First, the clarification that the *hon* and *soku* are difficult to fathom.

The Contemplation is divided into three parts: first, the title and general praise; second, the detailed explanation according to the sequence of the teachings; and third, the comprehensive manifestation of its meritorious excellence, followed by the discussion on the response to emotions. The first part [the title and general praise] is divided into two: first, the explanation of the title; and second, the general praise for its profound and mysterious purport.

The second part [the detailed explanation according to the sequence of the teachings] is divided into four: first, the phrase "Holy Wisdom" refers to the initial wisdom; second, the clarification of the Dharma-body; third, the teaching that is the ultimate resonance;

and fourth, the establishment of expedient means as being without deliberation. The third part [the comprehensive manifestation of its meritorious excellence] follows with the discussion on the response to emotions.

The false conceptualization is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the false conceptualization is divided into four sections: first, the section on wisdom beholding and responding with illumination; second, the section on the contemplation of the two bodies manifesting in accordance with forms;

third, the section on the teachings being revealed through the profound and relying upon [the capacity of beings]; and fourth, the section on expedient views shifting and changing. This concludes the general summary.

Next, the specific exposition of the arising of the teachings is divided into three parts: first, the gathering of those who are greatly benefited; second, the clarification of the teachings that benefit them; and third, the division of the teachings.
Third, the initial section clarifies the meaning of the five segments concerning the inconceivability of the Original [Vow] (hon) in common; this also serves as a conclusion.

Second, it clarifies the meaning of the six segments combined within the section on the inconceivability of the Traces (jaku); this likewise serves as a conclusion. Third, it clarifies the inconceivability of both the Original and the Traces together.

Third, it clarifies the reason for the threefold translation of the title of the sutra. This section is divided into four parts. First, it clarifies the translator of the sutra, which is divided into two parts. First, it introduces...
In the section "Praising the Virtues," five phrases are clarified; subsequently, within the section "Explaining the Intent of the Re-translation," four internal segments are clarified:

first, the time of the translation; second, the translator’s eightfold qualities. Regarding the first, "Praising the Virtues": "The Benevolent One" refers to Master Kumārajīva. "Praising the virtues" means his wisdom and loftiness;

"highly transcendent" means he surpassed those of the mundane world and attained transcendence. This concludes the praise of his virtues, followed by the explanation of the translation of the scriptures.
At that time, I held the Hu-language manuscript in my hand. Regarding the reason for the fourfold clarification of the *Dharmapada* commentary, it is divided into two parts.
First, the expression of humility: the six sections of text beginning with "I, by virtue of my ignorance and brevity... explain the intent of the subsequent clarification.
The phrase "I hope that future gentlemen... refers to the following words. The statement "In the second year of the Dali era" indicates when this was composed.
The "Preface" briefly records the dates; the monk Tiliqing who composed this preface was the nephew of the later Abbot of Zisheng Temple.
Having personally listened to and verified [the text] three times across the past and present, I ask future students not to harbor doubts.
Of the three sections, the first two—the "Tiantai" and "Past and Present"—have been explained above. Now, we shall proceed to the third: the formal explanation of the title of the sutra. Furthermore—
This title is briefly divided into two parts.
